title: Psalm 98: Victory, Music, and the Coming Judge
summary: The psalm calls for a new song because the LORD has won a victory and made his salvation known to the nations, remembering his love and faithfulness to Israel. All the earth is summoned to shout and play lyre, harp, trumpet, and ram's horn before the King. Then the sea, the rivers, and the mountains join in, because he is coming to judge the world with righteousness.
story: Psalm 98 belongs to the kingship psalms of Book IV and is a close sister of Psalm 96: both begin with a new song and end with nearly the same lines about the LORD coming to judge the earth. The difference is the reason for singing. Psalm 96 praised God as Creator above the idols; Psalm 98 praises him for something he has just done, a saving victory that the ends of the earth have seen. In the larger story of Book IV, which responds to the ruin of David's kingdom, that victory looks like the return from exile: God has acted for Israel in full view of the nations, and the whole world is invited to celebrate.
historical:
The Hebrew heading is a single word, mizmor, “A Psalm”, the only kingship psalm in this group with any heading, and it names no author or occasion. The psalm does not say what victory it celebrates. Many scholars read it against the return from Babylon after Cyrus of Persia allowed the exiles to go home in 539/538 BC, because its language closely matches Isaiah 52:10, where the LORD bares his holy arm before the nations and all the ends of the earth see the salvation of our God. Others hear the exodus behind it, since the right hand and holy arm are also images from the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:6, 12). Still others read it as a festival hymn that could celebrate any of God's great acts, past or yet to come.

Whatever its first occasion, the psalm was sung in temple worship with a full orchestra. The instruments it names were all in use in Israel's worship from the monarchy onward, and Chronicles describes Levites playing them before the ark (1 Chronicles 15:28).
cultural:
Victory songs were a familiar genre in the ancient world. When an army returned from battle, women came out with singing and dancing (Exodus 15:20-21; 1 Samuel 18:6), and kings commissioned inscriptions praising their triumphs. This psalm is a victory song for the LORD, the divine warrior whose “right hand and holy arm” (verse 1) have won, but the battle is never described. The spotlight is entirely on what the victory reveals: God's righteousness and his loyalty to Israel.

The instruments tell a story of their own. The lyre (kinnor) and harp were stringed instruments used in both worship and celebration. The trumpets were straight metal horns blown by priests (Numbers 10:1-10). The ram's horn, or shofar, was the signal horn of war and of coronation; it sounded when a king was proclaimed (1 Kings 1:39) and on solemn days such as the Day of Atonement in the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:9). To blow it “before the LORD, the King” (verse 6) was to hail him as newly enthroned.
literary: The psalm has three stanzas of roughly equal length, and each widens the circle of singers. Verses 1 to 3 give the reason for praise: the victory, told three times with salvation, righteousness, and faithfulness. Verses 4 to 6 summon all the earth to worship with voice and instruments, piling up verbs of shouting and singing. Verses 7 to 9 summon creation itself, with the lovely personification of rivers clapping their hands and mountains singing together. The Hebrew root for salvation appears three times in the first stanza (translated “victory” in verse 1 and “salvation” in verses 2 and 3), and the psalm closes almost word for word as Psalm 96 does, giving the two psalms a shared ending.

outline.t: The LORD's victory revealed to the nations
All the earth, sing and play before the King
Sea, rivers, and mountains welcome the Judge

doctrines.note: Salvation here is something God does, by his own right hand, and then makes public. It is rooted in his remembering his love and faithfulness to Israel, and its effects are seen by the ends of the earth.
Verse 3 grounds the victory in God's covenant: he “remembered His love and faithfulness to the house of Israel”. His saving acts are loyalty to promises already made.
As in Psalm 96, the coming of God to judge the world is cause for creation's joy, because his judgment is righteous and fair, setting right what has gone wrong.

words.note: Yeshuah, salvation or victory. It can mean military deliverance, rescue from danger, or well-being restored. The name Joshua, and its later form Jeshua, from which the name Jesus comes, is built on the same root.

Chesed, steadfast love or covenant loyalty, rendered “love” in verse 3. It is the kindness that keeps a commitment, and it is often paired, as here, with faithfulness. God's victory is not a random display of power but chesed in action.

Shophar, the ram's horn. Unlike the metal trumpets, it produced a few loud notes and served as a signal: for battle, for gathering the people, for proclaiming a king. Its use in this psalm is part of the coronation imagery.
Meshar, uprightness or equity, translated “equity” in verse 9. It describes what is level and straight, fairness without favoritism. The judge who comes will not tilt the scales.

christ: Many readers hear this psalm in the song of Mary, who praises God because he has helped his servant Israel, remembering his mercy (Luke 1:54), much as verse 3 says. The psalm's picture of the nations seeing God's salvation finds its answer when the old man Simeon holds the infant Jesus and says his eyes have seen God's salvation, prepared in the presence of all peoples (Luke 2:30-31). In the eighteenth century Isaac Watts paraphrased this psalm in the hymn known as Joy to the World, reading its coming King as Christ. The link is fulfillment rather than prediction in the narrow sense: the psalm celebrates God's saving victory for Israel before the nations, and the Gospels announce that victory arriving in a person.
questions: The psalm spends three verses on what God has done before it asks anyone to sing. Why might praise be stronger when it starts with remembering specific acts of God?
Rivers clapping and mountains singing are poetic, but the psalm means something by them. What does it suggest about God's purposes for the physical world?
What “new song” might you have reason to sing because of something God has done recently?
